tagline: One-lane bridges and rainforest bends link Maui’s north shore communities.
intro: The road to Hāna changes from a rural highway into a narrow mountain route, with one-lane bridges and stretches of one-lane roadway. Route 360 has approximately 620 curves, almost all through tropical rainforest. For the longer journey from Kahului, Wikipedia gives about 2.5 hours of uninterrupted driving, reflecting the narrow road and its winding course. In 2000, President Bill Clinton designated the highway the Hāna Millennium Legacy Trail, beginning at Pāʻia; it entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2001.

Modern road building began in the 1870s with an unpaved route for construction of the Hämäkua Ditch. The ditch carried water from Haleakalā’s rainforests to semi-arid central Maui for sugarcane cultivation. The road grew piecemeal until the full route opened in December 1926. Bridge construction continued through the 1930s, and complete paving waited until the 1960s.

From Pāʻia, Route 36 runs east through Haʻikū, becoming Route 360 east of Haʻikū at the Route 365 junction. Kaumahina State Wayside offers views of the northeast coast and Keʻanae Peninsula. Tourist guides use mile markers on Route 360, not those on Route 36. Continue toward Keʻanae, then Wailua and Nāhiku, before reaching Hāna at Route 360’s mile 34.

moments.title: Pāʻia
moments.text: Surf shops, galleries and restaurants occupy a town that housed a Hawaiian Commercial & Sugar Company mill from 1880 to 2000. Pāʻia is the first town encountered when traveling eastbound on the Hāna Highway, on Maui’s northern coast. At nearby Hoʻokipa, reefs across the bay shape the waves, while strong winds support windsurfing. Windsurfing and surfing competitions take place there, and the beach park beside the highway has observation decks. The waves are largest in winter and smaller in summer; the Aloha Classic is a long-running windsurfing competition held at Hoʻokipa.

moments.title: Keʻanae
moments.text: Taro is grown on Keʻanae’s peninsula, land formed from lava that originated at Haleakalā Crater. A stone church nearby, built in 1856, was among the few buildings left after the 1946 tsunami, which killed twenty-four people. Agricultural ground also underlies the nearby Keʻanae Arboretum: it occupies taro terraces beside Piinaau Stream. Before becoming an arboretum in 1971, the land grew food, medicine and fiber plants, then served as an agricultural work site for prisoners from 1946 into the mid-1950s. Labeled trees and two short walking trails now introduce visitors to native and introduced tropical plants there.

moments.title: Hāna
moments.text: The year 1946 brought a plantation closure and a new inn to Hāna. The last sugarcane plantation closed, and plantation workers moved mostly to western Maui. Paul Fagan opened the six-room Kaʻuiki Inn that year. In 1947, he brought his San Francisco Seals baseball team and sports journalists to Hāna for spring training to promote the destination. The inn developed into the Hāna-Maui Resort, which remains among the community’s overnight accommodations. A volcanic-rock cross on Lyon Hill commemorates Fagan; erected in 1960, it is a memorial rather than his burial place.
